title: Impact of BRT Corridor on Urban Commute Times

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID).

Why: The data contain a treated indicator (area ever exposed to the BRT corridor), a post indicator (periods after the corridor opened), and their interaction. These ingredients map directly into a DID design that compares the change in log-commute times in treated areas before vs. after opening to the contemporaneous change in control areas.

Key assumptions  
1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the BRT corridor, treated and control urban areas would have experienced the same trend in log-commute times.  
2. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers between areas).  
3. No other policy differentially coincides with “post” for treated areas.  

To bolster the parallel-trends assumption we add unit and period fixed effects and run a simple pre-trend (event-study) check as a robustness exercise.

---

## 2. R Code
```r
################################################################################
# Impact of BRT Corridor on Log–Commute Times
# Difference-in-Differences with robustness checks
################################################################################
# Load packages
required <- c("data.table", "fixest", "modelsummary")
invisible(lapply(required, require, character.only = TRUE))

# 1. Read the data -------------------------------------------------------------
df <- fread("experiments/exp_b/data/s48_data.csv")

# Ensure interaction is present (re-create to avoid mistakes)
df[, treat_x_post := treated * post]

# 2. Baseline DID with two-way fixed effects ----------------------------------
did <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
             data = df, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("\nBaseline DID result (clustered s.e. by unit):\n")
print(etable(did, se = "cluster"))

# 3. Robustness check 1: Event-study (lead/lag) --------------------------------
# All areas adopt at the same time -> relative period = period - first treated‐post period
first_post_period <- min(df[post == 1, period])
df[, reltime := period - first_post_period]        # t = 0 is the first post period

# Build dummies for leads (-3,-2,-1) and lags (0,+1,+2,+3)
window <- -3:3
for (k in window) df[, paste0("D", k) := as.integer(reltime == k & treated == 1)]

# Omit D-1 to serve as baseline
leadlag_fml <- as.formula(paste(
  "y ~", paste(paste0("D", window[window != -1]), collapse = " + "),
  "| unit_id + period"))

event <- feols(leadlag_fml, data = df, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("\nEvent-study (lead/lag) estimates relative to period ‑1:\n")
print(etable(event, se = "cluster"))

# 4. Robustness check 2: Placebo – pretend the BRT opened one period earlier ---
df[, placebo_post := as.integer(period >= (first_post_period - 1))]
df[, placebo_treat_x_post := treated * placebo_post]

placebo <- feols(y ~ placebo_treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
                 data = df, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("\nPlacebo test (fake opening one period early):\n")
print(etable(placebo, se = "cluster"))

# 5. Compact numerical output for replication logs -----------------------------
cat("\n--- Key numbers -----------------------------------------------------------\n")
cat("Baseline DID coefficient (treat_x_post): ",
    coef(did)["treat_x_post"], "\n")
cat("Std. error (clustered): ",
    se(did, "cluster")["treat_x_post"], "\n")
cat("Placebo coefficient: ",
    coef(placebo)["placebo_treat_x_post"], "\n")
cat("-------------------------------------------------------------------------\n")
```

---

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Negative. A BRT corridor should reduce average commute times; since the dependent variable is the log of commute time, we expect a decline (negative coefficient) for treated × post.

Magnitude: A plausible reduction of roughly 5–10 percent. Thus the DID coefficient on treat_x_post is expected around −0.05 to −0.10 (i.e., exp(−0.05)=0.95, a 5 % fall in commute times).

Confidence: If the parallel-trends assumption holds, the event-study leads (pre-treatment coefficients) should be statistically indistinguishable from zero, reinforcing causal interpretation.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in commute times between treated and untreated areas over time.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The opening of a BRT corridor is associated with an increase in the log of commute times.
